fields.meta_title: Community Survey Builder for Local Groups | Emergent
fields.meta_description: Create a community survey for your town or neighborhood group: rank local projects, split answers by area, and own every response.
fields.h1: Build a Community Survey for Your Town or Group
fields.hero_description: Build a community survey residents can answer on their phones, with every response saved to a database you own.
fields.features_heading: What Residents See and Your Team Reads
fields.features_subheading: Residents meet the first three on a phone. Your team works in the last three, from the first split result to the exported code.
fields.feature_1:
Questions that rank or rate

Emergent writes each question in the type the decision needs. Residents drag park projects into order or rate trash pickup on a 1-5 scale, and each answer gets its own column.
fields.feature_2:
One question per screen on a phone

Anyone who opens the link on a phone sees one question at a time, with a progress bar that counts what is left. On a laptop, the same survey can run as a single scrolling page.
fields.feature_3:
Reminders to households yet to answer

Give each household its own survey link and the app knows who has answered. On the day you pick, it emails a reminder to the rest and skips anyone whose answers are in.
fields.feature_4:
Results split by neighborhood or branch

Add a field for neighborhood or library branch, and the dashboard breaks every result down by it. A project that wins across town but loses on the east side shows at once.
fields.feature_5:
Every answer in a database you own

Each response is a row in your own database, with the area and the date beside every answer. Filter it for a council memo, or connect it by API to the tools you already use.
fields.feature_6:
Code you can move to your own GitHub

On paid plans, Emergent exports the full survey app, with its logic and dashboard, to your GitHub repository. Your IT team can review the code or keep building on it later.

fields.usecase_heading: Four Local Teams With a Decision to Make
fields.tab_content_1:
472 first-choice votes go to the Miller Field splash pad

Ashgrove's parks department lists 4 projects it can fund and asks residents to rank them. After 1,180 residents answer, the dashboard counts first choices. The Miller Field splash pad leads with 472, and trail lighting is second at 354.
fields.tab_content_2:
Westside alone says yes to Sunday hours

Cedar Mill Public Library asks card holders at its 3 branches whether to add Sunday hours, and the answers split by branch. Westside says yes 146 of 214 times, while Downtown and Orchard Park both lean no. Branch manager Ines Halvorsen drafts a Sunday schedule for her branch only.
fields.tab_content_3:
A day-7 reminder goes to 244 quiet households

Fernhill's board sends its survey on a new Alder Street crosswalk to 340 households, each with its own link. In the first week, 96 answer. On day 7, the app emails a reminder to the 244 households that have not answered and leaves the rest alone.
fields.tab_content_4:
Saturday morning wins, with answers in English or Spanish

Riverbend Food Pantry hands clients a QR code in the pickup line. The survey opens on their phone in English or Spanish, one question per screen. On question 4 of 6, the pickup time, Saturday morning leads with 58 of 122 answers, and Tuesday evening follows at 41.

fields.howto_title: How to Create a Community Survey
fields.howto_description: Seven steps to build a community survey with Emergent and read every answer by neighborhood once it closes.
fields.howto_step_3_title: 03 Pick a type for each question
fields.howto_step_1_des: Name the decision the survey feeds before you write a single question: which park project to fund, or whether to open on Sundays. Cut every question that does not move that decision. What is left is the outline for your prompt.
fields.howto_step_2_des: Type the survey in plain English, naming who answers and what the results page should show. Emergent builds the survey and its database from that description, along with the dashboard. To change a question later, ask for the change in a sentence.
fields.howto_step_3_des: Use a ranking when residents choose between projects and a 1-5 scale when they rate a service. A single proposal like Sunday hours needs only a yes or no. Put one open box last, for anything your list missed.
fields.howto_step_4_des: Ask for the neighborhood or branch near the start, as a pick list instead of a typed answer. That one field lets the dashboard split every result by area, which is where a townwide average can hide a split between two sides of town.
fields.howto_step_5_des: Send the link to five people who did not help write it, and ask at least two of them to answer on a phone. Watch for any question they read two ways or skip, and reword it before the real launch.
fields.howto_step_6_title: 06 Publish and hand out the link
fields.howto_step_6_des: Publish the survey on its own link or on your town's domain, and print the link as a QR code for flyers at the library desk and the pickup line. Give each household a personal link if you plan to send reminders.
fields.howto_step_7_title: 07 Remind once and read the results
fields.howto_step_7_des: Pick a reminder day about a week in, and the app emails only the households that have not answered. When the survey closes, read the results by area and tell the people who answered what you decided.

faq_plan.a: A community survey is a set of questions a town, library, neighborhood group, or nonprofit puts to the people it serves. Their answers settle a local decision, such as moving a bus stop or adding a market day. It is not the American Community Survey, which is conducted by the Census Bureau.

faq_plan.q: How do I create a community survey?
faq_plan.a: Start in Emergent's AI survey builder with a prompt that names the decision, the people answering, and the area field you will split results by. Emergent builds the survey from that prompt, with its database and dashboard. Then take it yourself on a phone before anyone else sees the link.

faq_plan.q: Which community survey questions should a local group ask first?
faq_plan.a: Ask first about the decision the survey exists to make, then where the person lives, and save age or household size for the end. Good community survey questions name one thing each: "Rank these 4 projects" beats "How do you feel about parks and roads?" Ask for demographics only when a result will be split by them.

faq_plan.q: What are good community survey examples for a small town?
faq_plan.a: Good ones each feed a single decision, like a transit survey on moving a bus stop or a downtown survey on closing Main Street to cars on Saturdays. Both community survey examples keep the list short and end in one choice. When the goal is to find unmet needs before a grant application, run a needs assessment survey instead.

faq_plan.q: Is a community survey template worth using, or should I write my own?
faq_plan.a: Use a template for the order and write the questions yourself. A community survey template gets the sequence right: the decision first, the area field next, one open box last. Only you can name your projects and your streets. Emergent builds the survey from your description. The prompt does the job a template would.

faq_plan.q: How many questions should a community survey have?
faq_plan.hint: How to create and publish community survey questions?
faq_plan.a: Keep it to 12 questions or fewer, short enough to finish in about 5 minutes on a phone. Each extra question is one more reason for a busy resident to stop halfway. If two questions would feed the same chart, keep the clearer one.

faq_plan.q: Can a local business use a community survey to test demand?
faq_plan.a: Yes, for a narrow local question, such as whether neighbors would shop at a weekday farmers market. A community survey asks residents about a shared place or service. To price a product or size a market, a market research survey fits better, since its questions are about buying.

faq_plan.q: How do I get more residents to answer community surveys?
faq_plan.a: Ask in person where people already gather, such as the senior center or a school pickup line, and keep a few paper copies to type in later. Say on the first screen what the answers will decide and by when. Surveys built on Emergent have no response cap. A big turnout keeps counting.

faq_plan.q: Should a community survey be anonymous?
faq_plan.a: Make it anonymous when the topic is sensitive, and use personal links only when you need reminders. Answers that come in through a personal link are tied to a household and are not anonymous. A middle path is to ask only for the neighborhood. On Emergent, every answer lands in a database your group owns.

faq_plan.q: Should a community survey ask residents about their well-being?
faq_plan.a: Only when the decision needs it, and then with 1 or 2 optional questions. A survey on park projects can ask how often people exercise outdoors, but keep the topic narrow. For a full picture of how people sleep and manage stress, run a separate wellness survey and keep it anonymous.

plan.angle: The top 10 is the Census Bureau's American Community Survey and institutional toolkits (HUD, Polco's national benchmark, a how-to guide); none lets a town, library, neighborhood association or nonprofit build its own community survey and keep the answers. This page is for that local team: rank projects, split answers by branch or area, remind the households that have not answered, and run it on a phone one question at a time, with every answer a row in a database the team owns. The FAQ answers the questions a local organizer asks before launch (which questions, how many, anonymity, reaching more residents), and the definition says in one sourced line that the Census Bureau's survey is a different thing.

scope.evidence: H1 'Build a Community Survey for Your Town or Group', title 'Community Survey Builder for Local Groups | Emergent' and hero 'Build a community survey residents can answer on their phones, with every response saved to a database you own.' state the whole job; howto_description is one sentence.

intent.evidence: AMBER: the SERP is the Census Bureau's ACS plus institutional how-to toolkits, with no builder in the top 10. The page carries its angle (local teams building their own survey) and serves the ACS searcher with four sourced answers: FAQ 1 what it is, FAQ 3 mandatory, FAQ 5 what it asks, FAQ 6 confidentiality, each saying a local survey is a different thing ('It is a national program, separate from the local community surveys a town or nonprofit runs'). The how-to covers the conduct-a-survey guides.

specificity.evidence: Local-team vocabulary: park projects ranked, branches, households with their own link, a pantry pickup line QR code, 'a council memo', 'the meeting where the decision gets made'.

openers.evidence: Paragraphs open on full sentences: 'Ashgrove's parks department lists 4 projects...', 'Riverbend Food Pantry hands clients a QR code...', 'Name the decision the survey feeds...'.

craft.evidence: One idea per sentence ('In the first week, 96 answer.'); a tacked-on 'which is where' clause in step 4 is a note.

voice.evidence: Concrete and calm: 'A project that wins across town but loses on the east side shows at once.' No AI tells.

truth.evidence: Every ACS line stays inside its census.gov quote: 'about 3.5 million addresses each year', 'required by law (Title 13, U.S. Code, Sections 141, 193, and 221)', 'Title 13, as changed by Title 18, imposes a penalty', 'Title 13, Section 9', 'not any other federal agencies, outside organizations, or law enforcement', 'about 40 minutes'. Emergent lines map to prompt-build, conversational, alerts, database-owned, api-connect, no-caps, code-export, free-start, custom-domain. Numbers add up: 472+354+236+118 = 1,180; 146/214 = 68%; 96+244 = 340; 58+41+23 = 122.

distinct.evidence: No sibling primary (needs assessment survey, demographic survey, market research survey) headlined or answered; church, brand perception and pulse survey are only linked.

faq.evidence: 10 on-topic questions answered first-sentence; hub link in item 2; three sibling links (brand perception survey, church survey, pulse survey); no brand or file format in a question; all four secondaries carried.

images.evidence: Contact sheet matches the tabs: bars 472/354/236/118 with 1,180 responses; branch table Westside 214/146/68%; steps 'First week 96 answered', 'Reminder emailed 244 households Day 7'; phone 'Question 4 of 6', English/Spanish, bars 58/41/23 with '122 answers'.
